recall.question: What is the feature-map idea?
recall.answer: Map the input x to phi(x) listing the nonlinear terms, then fit a linear model in the features. The model did not change. The input did.

recall.question: In the computed example, what is phi(2) and the prediction?
recall.answer: phi(2) = [1, 2, 4, 8]. With theta = [1, 0.5, -0.1, 0.02] the prediction is 1.76.

sections.title: SL-02: The dual representation and kernelized LMS

keyTerms.definition: theta = sum_i beta_i phi(x^{(i)}): a combination of training feature vectors.
K(x, z) = phi(x)^T phi(z), the inner product we never form.
K, the matrix of all pairwise K(x^{(i)}, x^{(j)}).
The dual coefficients, one per training example.

recall.question: What is the kernel trick?
recall.answer: Predictions need only inner products phi(x)^T phi(z). Define K(x, z) as that inner product and never form phi.

recall.question: What is the kernelized LMS update?
recall.answer: beta_i := beta_i + alpha (y^{(i)} - sum_j beta_j K(x^{(i)}, x^{(j)})), or beta := beta + alpha (y - K beta).

recall.question: Why does the dual win when p >> n?
recall.answer: It trades feature dimension for sample size: beta has length n (examples), not p (features). It wins when p >> n and loses when n >> p.

sections.title: SL-03: Gram matrices and valid kernels

keyTerms.definition: K_ij = K(x^{(i)}, x^{(j)}): all pairwise similarities.
Symmetric positive semidefinite: necessary for a valid kernel.
Symmetric PSD on every finite point set means some phi exists.

recall.question: Why must a kernel matrix be symmetric PSD?
recall.answer: If K comes from some phi, K is symmetric (inner products commute) and PSD (z^T K z is a sum of squares). Mercer says the converse holds.

recall.question: Why is K(x,z) = x - z invalid?
recall.answer: On points {0,1} the matrix [[0,-1],[1,0]] is not symmetric. Rejected.

recall.question: What breaks with a non-PSD hand-made similarity?
recall.answer: The dual objective is no longer convex, SMO-style solvers can diverge, and predictions lose meaning.

sections.title: SL-04: Geometry, costs, regularization, scaling, limits

keyTerms.definition: Ridge on beta (add lambda I to K), or picking sigma by validation.
Standardize first, then pick sigma on the standardized scale.
O(n) per query: every query touches all support points.

recall.question: What does the dual cost?
recall.answer: Gram matrix: O(n^2) kernel evaluations and O(n^2) memory. Kernelized LMS per sweep: O(n^2). Prediction per query: O(n).

recall.question: In the cost example, why is the primal cheaper?
recall.answer: n = 10,000, d = 20, degree 3: the Gram is 1e8 entries (800 MB) and one beta sweep is 1e8 multiply-adds. Explicit features give p ~ 1771 and a primal sweep of 1.8e7. n >> p, so the dual loses.

recall.question: Why must features be standardized for the Gaussian kernel?
recall.answer: K is ruled by raw distances: dollars vs cents gets 1e4 times the weight. Standardize first, then pick sigma.
